title: Personalized NEXT25 Blueprint™
subtitle: A field guide for the next chapter
executive: Michael does not appear to need a single replacement career. His strongest pattern points toward a deliberately designed portfolio: selective advisory work that uses accumulated judgment, a teaching component that turns experience into a repeatable asset, and enough open capacity for travel, family and curiosity. The central design challenge is not capability. It is preventing a promising next chapter from recreating the time pressure, organizational politics and constant availability of the role he is leaving.
noticed: He still wants difficult problems, but not an always-on executive identity.
Teaching and mentoring are energizing when the group is purposeful.
Cold prospecting is likely to be a friction point, not proof that ownership is unsuitable.
Optional earned income matters, but freedom is a co-equal objective.
workstyle: Prefer purposeful interaction over continuous networking.
Design referral-led acquisition before cold outbound.
tensions: Expertise leverage vs. desire not to recreate old identity
Entrepreneurial autonomy vs. dislike of continuous selling
Meaningful engagement vs. protecting unstructured time
nine: Learning Sabbatical with Published Field Notes

briefs.title: Fractional Operations & Strategy Adviser
why: Leverages Michael’s accumulated operating judgment rather than requiring a complete retraining.
Can be structured around a small number of bounded client engagements, supporting autonomy and a 15–25 hour target.
The main friction is business development, so the operating model should emphasize warm introductions, referral partners and a narrow expertise proposition rather than high-volume cold outreach.
reality: Diagnose operating bottlenecks and decision problems
Translate findings into a short action roadmap
Check progress on a limited cadence rather than becoming the de facto full-time executive
briefs.friction: Selling/prospecting may drain energy. Design around it with former-colleague introductions, CPA/attorney/banker referral relationships, selective speaking, and a small target-account list.
briefs.income: Closest BLS occupational benchmark: Management Analysts. May 2025 median annual employee wage was $101,860; lowest 10% below $60,640 and highest 10% above $171,640. BLS also notes self-employed analysts are typically paid by the hour or project. These employee wage statistics do not establish consulting revenue or owner income.
business_model: Fractional retainer: limited monthly availability with explicit boundaries
market: Former employers, vendors and industry peers with 20–250 employees
Lower-middle-market owners facing growth, process or succession complexity
Referral partners: CPAs, attorneys, commercial bankers, benefits/HR advisers
Industry associations and private peer groups
Selective workshops built around one operational problem
first30: Write a one-sentence problem statement: who Michael helps, with what problem, and what changes after the engagement.
List 20 people who have previously sought Michael’s judgment; select 8 for learning conversations.
Interview 5 owner/executive prospects about their current operational bottlenecks—do not pitch first.
Draft one fixed-scope diagnostic offer with deliverables, time boundary and a test price.
Ask 3 potential referral partners what client situations would cause them to make an introduction.
briefs.experiment: Within 90 days, complete 8–10 discovery conversations, secure at least one bounded paid or deliberately unpaid pilot, deliver it, and record four pieces of evidence: customer value, personal energy, tolerance for business development, and willingness to repeat the work.
wrong: If Michael strongly dislikes even relationship-based business development
If client deadlines recreate the corporate pressure he wants to leave
If buyers consistently want full-time execution rather than advisory judgment

briefs.title: Executive Workshop & Leadership Lab
why: Matches teaching/mentoring energy and converts expertise into a repeatable intellectual asset.
Allows controlled scheduling and can complement, rather than replace, advisory work.
Creates a lower-pressure way to become visible to potential advisory clients.
reality: Design a 60–120 minute workshop around a narrow executive problem
Use cases/exercises rather than generic lectures
Offer follow-on working sessions only when desired
fit: Moderate visibility rather than constant networking
briefs.friction: Requires some public visibility. Begin with invited small groups, partner-hosted sessions, or private company workshops rather than large-stage speaking.
briefs.income: Treat workshop economics as a business scenario, not a salary forecast. Example only: 2 workshops/month × an illustrative $2,500 fee × 10 active months = $50,000 gross revenue before preparation, marketing, travel, taxes and other costs. Pricing must be validated with actual buyers before it is treated as market evidence.
market: Accounting, law, banking or benefits firms seeking client education
Executive peer groups and local business organizations
first30: Choose one problem Michael can teach without extensive new research.
Create a one-page workshop promise, three learning outcomes and a 60-minute outline.
Ask 5 potential hosts whether the topic would be useful to their members/clients/team.
Deliver one invitation-only pilot to 6–12 people.
Collect structured feedback on relevance, energy, clarity and follow-up demand.
briefs.experiment: Deliver two small-group pilots within 90 days. Continue only if participants report a specific useful outcome and Michael finds the preparation/facilitation energizing enough to repeat.
wrong: If preparation time overwhelms delivery time
If visibility feels draining even in small groups
If buyers value the topic but will not sponsor or pay for it

briefs.title: Niche Research & Executive Briefing Practice
why: Strong fit with analytical depth and deliberate pace.
Could create a lower-social-intensity portfolio component.
Can support advisory or workshop work with proprietary insight.
reality: Offer private briefings or commissioned research
briefs.friction: Monetization may be slower and requires proof that a narrow audience will pay for synthesis rather than obtain information free elsewhere.
briefs.income: No defensible single income benchmark is assumed. Revenue should be modeled from subscribers, commissioned briefs or briefing engagements only after buyer interviews establish willingness to pay.
first30: Choose one narrow question worth tracking for 90 days.
Interview 5 executives about what information they cannot easily synthesize.
Ask interviewees what would make it valuable enough to pay for or sponsor.
briefs.experiment: Publish one sample and conduct 8 buyer interviews; proceed only if a specific paid use case emerges.
wrong: If research becomes interesting but commercially unnecessary
If Michael wants more human interaction than the model provides
If the niche is too broad to create differentiated insight

gap: Michael may be searching for a job-shaped answer to a portfolio-shaped life.
The overlooked opportunity is not necessarily a new occupation; it may be a designed combination of advisory, teaching, research and deliberately protected freedom.
plan90: Weeks 1–2: choose two hypotheses to test; write narrow problem statements.
Weeks 2–5: conduct 8–10 buyer/host interviews across warm contacts and referral partners.
Weeks 4–8: run one advisory diagnostic and one workshop pilot.
Weeks 8–10: review evidence—energy, demand, economics, schedule impact, selling tolerance.
Weeks 10–12: choose continue / redesign / stop for each path; build the next experiment rather than a permanent commitment.
